title: Input output values and rules

worked_examples.q: A flow machine multiplies each input by 3. Find the output for input 4.

steps.title: Track the input
steps.action: Move the four tile into the multiplication box.
steps.narration: The given input is four.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.action: Four groups of three give twelve.
steps.narration: The output is twelve, not seven.

worked_examples.repair: Read the operation printed inside the flow box.

worked_examples.q: The flow is add 5, then double. Find the output when the input is 2.

steps.title: First arrow
steps.action: Two plus five gives seven.
steps.narration: Do the operation beside the first arrow first.

steps.title: Second arrow
steps.action: Double seven to fourteen.
steps.narration: The doubling applies to seven, not two.

worked_examples.repair: Place the intermediate result between the two arrows.

worked_examples.skill: Find a missing output from a table
worked_examples.q: A rule is y=x+4. A table contains input 1→5 and 3→7. Find the missing output for input 6.

model.description: Find a missing output from a table

states: Rule x+4 with missing row x=6

steps.title: Choose the missing row
steps.action: Move input six into the rule.
steps.narration: The other rows show how the rule behaves.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.action: Add four to six to get ten.
steps.narration: Check the same add-four pattern holds for all rows.

worked_examples.misconception: Copying the previous output rather than applying the rule.
worked_examples.repair: Trace the input row through the rule.

worked_examples.q: A multiply-by-4 machine produces output 28. What input did it receive?

steps.title: Read the output backward
steps.action: Start at twenty eight and undo multiplication by four.
steps.narration: The reverse action is division.

steps.title: Recover the input
steps.action: Twenty eight shared into four groups gives seven.
steps.narration: Send seven forward to check.

worked_examples.repair: Use an inverse arrow from output to input.

worked_examples.q: A machine triples a number then adds 2. Its output is 20. Find the input.

steps.title: Undo the last action
steps.action: Subtract two from twenty.
steps.narration: Reverse the operations in the opposite order.

steps.title: Undo the first action
steps.action: Divide eighteen by three.
steps.narration: Six is the original input.

worked_examples.misconception: Dividing twenty by three before removing the two.
worked_examples.repair: Walk back through the flow boxes from right to left.

worked_examples.skill: Read a rule from constant differences
worked_examples.q: A table shows input 0,1,2,3 and output 5,8,11,14. Give the rule.

model.description: Read a rule from constant differences

steps.title: Compare two adjacent rows
steps.action: The output rises by three whenever the input rises by one.
steps.narration: Three is the multiplier of x.

steps.title: Find the start
steps.action: The row at input zero gives five.
steps.narration: Five is the fixed part.

steps.title: Join rule parts
steps.action: Multiply input by three, then add five.
steps.narration: Check all four rows.

worked_examples.misconception: Calling five the multiplier because it is the first output.
worked_examples.repair: Use the input-zero row for the fixed term.

worked_examples.q: The rule y=2x−3 maps x=−2 to an output. Find it and show the signed substitution.

steps.title: Keep negative input grouped
steps.action: Two times negative two is negative four.
steps.narration: Brackets protect the sign of the input.

steps.title: Subtract three
steps.action: Move three more units left from negative four.
steps.narration: The output is negative seven.

worked_examples.misconception: Treating negative two as positive two.
worked_examples.repair: Place a signed tile into the input slot.

worked_examples.q: Flow A doubles x then adds 3. Flow B adds 3 then doubles. Find both outputs at x=4.
states: One input four; two different flows

steps.title: Trace flow A
steps.action: Double four to eight, then add three to eleven.
steps.narration: Keep the order stated for A.

steps.title: Trace flow B
steps.action: Add three to four to make seven, then double to fourteen.
steps.narration: Do not reuse A’s intermediate value.

worked_examples.misconception: Assuming the same numbers imply the same rule.
worked_examples.repair: Put each flow in a separate lane and compare outputs.

worked_examples.q: A table pairs x=1,2,3 with y=4,7,10. A learner proposes y=3x+1. Does the rule match every row?

steps.title: Check the first two rows
steps.action: Substitute one and two into the proposed formula.
steps.narration: Matching one row alone is insufficient.

steps.title: Check the remaining row
steps.action: Substitute three to get ten.
steps.narration: Every provided row must agree.

worked_examples.misconception: Declaring equivalence from a single matched row.

worked_examples.q: A taxi charges R7 when you board and R5 per kilometre. Build a rule and give fares for 0,2,4 km.
states: One boarding fee plus five per kilometre

steps.title: Count kilometre tiles
steps.action: Five rand repeats for each kilometre.
steps.narration: The boarding fee does not repeat.

steps.title: Add the start fee
steps.action: Keep seven rand once outside the repeated row.
steps.narration: This gives the rule seven plus five d.

steps.title: Complete table
steps.action: Evaluate the rule at zero, two and four kilometres.
steps.narration: Each two kilometres raises the fare by ten rand.

worked_examples.verify: At 4 km, 7+4×5=27 rand; zero-distance fare is R7.
worked_examples.misconception: Multiplying the once-only boarding fee by distance.
worked_examples.repair: Show fixed and variable charges in different rows.

worked_examples.q: A photo booth charges R6 once plus R4 per print. The total was R30. Find the number of prints.

steps.title: Remove the fixed charge
steps.action: Subtract the one six-rand fee from thirty.
steps.narration: Twenty four rand belongs to prints.

steps.title: Count print groups
steps.action: Divide twenty four by four rand per print.
steps.narration: The quotient is six prints.

worked_examples.misconception: Dividing the full total by the print price.
worked_examples.repair: Separate the fixed fee before reversing the flow.

worked_examples.q: A table pairs x=0,1,2,3 with y=0,1,4,9. Is y=2x a rule? Find a matching rule and output at x=4.

steps.title: Test the claim
steps.action: At one, the proposed double rule gives two.
steps.narration: The table actually shows one, so this rule fails.

steps.title: Test square rule
steps.action: Zero, one, four and nine are squares of the inputs.
steps.narration: Every given row agrees.

steps.title: Extend to four
steps.action: Four squared is sixteen.
steps.narration: This relationship is not a constant three-step increase.

worked_examples.misconception: Assuming any growing table is linear.
worked_examples.repair: Show square tiles growing by unequal amounts.

worked_examples.q: Plan A costs R12 plus R3 per visit; Plan B costs R6 per visit. Compare at 2 and 5 visits.

steps.title: Compare at two
steps.action: Calculate both plans for the same two visits.
steps.narration: B costs less at two.

steps.title: Compare at five
steps.action: Recalculate both plans for five visits.
steps.narration: A costs less at five; comparisons depend on input.

worked_examples.misconception: Assuming one plan is always cheaper.
worked_examples.repair: Keep both rules and both shared inputs visible.

worked_examples.q: A carton holds 6 eggs. Write E(c) and state sensible inputs for c cartons. How many eggs in 7 cartons?
worked_examples.answer: E(c)=6c eggs for whole-number c≥0; E(7)=42 eggs.
states: Only whole c≥0 describes complete cartons

steps.title: Build equal groups
steps.action: Place six eggs in every carton group.
steps.narration: The count follows six times c.

steps.title: Restrict input
steps.action: A complete carton count is a nonnegative whole number.
steps.narration: Half a carton is not a complete carton in this model.

steps.title: Evaluate seven
steps.action: Seven groups of six contain forty two eggs.
steps.narration: The output is an egg count.

worked_examples.repair: Show physical whole cartons, then name the domain.

worked_examples.q: A rule triples the input then subtracts 4. Fill outputs at x=−1,0,3, then recover the input whose output is 17.
states: Flow triples x then subtracts four

steps.title: Write the rule
steps.action: Place multiplication by three before subtraction of four.
steps.narration: The order is stated in the flow.

steps.title: Fill two rows
steps.action: At negative one output negative seven; at zero output negative four.
steps.narration: Keep the signed input when multiplying.

steps.title: Fill third row
steps.action: Three triples to nine then minus four leaves five.
steps.narration: Each row follows the same rule.

steps.title: Reverse the last arrow
steps.action: Add four to seventeen to recover twenty one.
steps.narration: Undo subtraction before multiplication.

steps.title: Reverse multiplication
steps.action: Divide twenty one by three to recover seven.
steps.narration: Run seven forward to verify.

worked_examples.repair: Preserve intermediate values in forward and reverse lanes.

practice_questions: For y=x+7, find the output at x=5.
A machine multiplies by 5 and outputs 35. Find the input.
Double then add 3 gives 19. Find the input.
Outputs rise by 4 for each input +1; at zero output is 2.
For y=3x+1, find output at x=−2.
A doubles x then subtracts 1; B subtracts 1 then doubles. Give outputs at x=3.
A club costs R9 once and R4 per session. Give C(s) and C(3).
R5 once plus R3 per item totals R20. Find items.
Table x=0,1,2 gives y=0,1,4. Find rule and y at x=3.
A=R8+R2 per visit; B=R5 per visit. Compare 2 and 4 visits.
At two B is cheaper; at four A is cheaper.
Five buttons per completed card. Write B(c), sensible c and B(8).
Eight groups of five give forty buttons.
Flow multiply by 4 then minus 3. Give outputs at −1 and 2, and input for output 17.
mastery_questions: Machine adds 6. What input gives output 13?
Difference is 3; input zero gives starting value 4.
Flow doubles then subtracts 5. Find output for x=−2 and input for output 11.
A delivery charges R10 once plus R6 per km. Give C(d), costs at 0 and 3 km, and sensible d.
The fixed charge is R10; 3 km adds R18; distance cannot be negative.
Plan A is R8+R4 per visit and Plan B is R6 per visit. Compare at 2 and 5 visits, with both formulas.
For two visits B costs R4 less. For five A costs R2 less; both calculations use the same input.
reassessment_questions: Add 7 then triple gives 30. Find the input.
Table 0→6,1→10,2→14. Write the rule and output for 4.
The output rises by 4 per input step and starts at 6.
A printer costs R5 once plus R2 per page. Write C(p), find C(6), and state a sensible domain.
C(p)=5+2p; C(6)=R17; p a whole number ≥0.
Six pages cost R12 plus one R5 fee; page count is nonnegative whole.
